title: Painted beams
hookLine: he had favorite sayings from the Bible and the classics painted on his library beams

cards: A sticky note on a bathroom mirror. A line of a poem taped above a kitchen sink. A grandmother's handwriting on an index card, stuck to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon.
People put words where their eyes will land when they're not trying to read. Montaigne did it too, but with paint, and overhead.
Lie on the floor of his tower library and look up, and the wooden beams of the ceiling are covered in sentences.

teach.b: First, the ceiling. Montaigne had short sayings painted along the beams and rafters of his library, in Latin and in Greek, the languages of the books on his shelves.
Every time he looked up from his writing, a line was waiting. Second, whose lines.
Scripture and the classics sit side by side. Some come from books like Ecclesiastes, with its long hard look at how little lasts. Some come from the old Roman and Greek writers.

One, borrowed from the Roman playwright Terence, says in Latin: I am a human being, and nothing human is foreign to me. Picture that over your desk while you write about your own kidney stones and your own bad moods.
It's almost permission. Third, why borrow at all. Montaigne's pages are full of other people's lines.

In his essay on educating children, he gives his reason: he quotes others only to say himself better. The beams weren't decoration. They were company, voices to argue with and lean on, sitting just above his head.
Fourth, the beams at home. No ceiling or paintbrush needed.

teach.h: ONE LINE WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT.
teach.b: One sentence, put where the eye lands without hunting for it, does a slow kind of work.
On a good day, it may get a nod. On a bad day, it can say something else. Given time, it stops being words on a card and starts being a voice in the room.

how: Some readers of Montaigne point to the painted beams of his library as a habit worth borrowing: keeping a few chosen sayings where the eye falls during an ordinary day.

games.q: you're Montaigne, writing alone in your tower. you want the old voices close while you work. what do you do?
o: paint their sayings on the ceiling beams.
hire a reader to recite to you all day.

games.why: he had sayings painted along the beams of his library, so when he looked up from the page, a line was waiting.

practice: Let a line come to mind that you already carry: a verse, a poem, a thing your grandfather used to say, even a line from a day on this path. Don't hunt for the best one; take the one that shows up.
Hold it for a few breaths, the way Montaigne could look up and find his beams.
